analysis.one_liner: Requires two-person freight crews, slower speeds for hazardous trains, more defect detectors, and bigger fines for railroads.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House bill to tighten railroad safety rules — including a two-person crew requirement and higher fines for violations — never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a series of high-profile derailments, this bill would require most large freight trains to carry at least a two-person crew, cap train speeds at 50 mph (40 mph in high-threat urban areas for trains loaded with flammable liquids), phase out older tank cars that rupture easily, and require the big freight railroads to install and maintain wayside defect detectors that catch overheated bearings before trains derail. It would also raise the maximum civil fine for rail safety violations to $5 million when someone is killed or badly hurt, require railroads to share train contents with first responders, and fund grade-crossing improvements and emergency responder training.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along freight rail lines — including in towns like East Palestine, Ohio — get stronger protections against derailments of trains carrying oil, chemicals, and explosives. Rail workers get guaranteed time to do safety inspections, protection against being pressured to sign off on unchecked repairs, and a confidential system for reporting close calls. Drivers and pedestrians get a toll-free number to report blocked grade crossings and more funding to eliminate dangerous ones. First responders get real-time information about what hazardous materials are on any train in their area.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail-line communities, rail workers, first responders

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars freight trains of the largest railroads from running without at least a two-person crew — a conductor and an engineer — with no exception for hazardous trains or trains longer than 7,500 feet.

It directs the Transportation Secretary to cap all trains at 50 mph, and to hold trains carrying 20 or more loaded flammable-liquid tank cars to 40 mph in high-threat urban areas unless every tank car meets the tougher DOT-117 safety standard.

It raises civil penalties for rail safety violations to a range of $5,000 to $1 million per violation, and up to $5 million when a violation kills or seriously injures someone; it also lets the Secretary double penalties for repeated or deliberate violations, and makes each day of a violation a separate offense.

It requires the largest railroads to adopt defect-detector networks with spacing standards designed to catch overheated wheel bearings — the failure that caused the East Palestine derailment — before the condition causes an accident, with federal approval, compliance reviews, and fines for noncompliance.

It requires Class I railroads to generate real-time electronic records of what hazardous materials each train carries, share them with fusion centers and state emergency commissions, and prohibits withholding that information from first responders during an incident.

It prohibits railroads from limiting the time employees have to complete railcar, locomotive, and brake inspections, and directs federal audits of whether railroad managers coerce workers into signing off on inspections or repairs.
It requires every Class I railroad and Amtrak to enroll in a confidential close-call reporting system for two years, and subjects inspection employees to alcohol and drug testing.

It phases out older, less protective tank cars (DOT-105, 111, 112, and 120 types) from carrying flammable liquids in packing groups II and III by December 31, 2027, unless they meet the tougher DOT-117, 117P, or 117R standards, with a one-year delay possible if manufacturing capacity falls short.

It requires every railroad to staff a toll-free number for reporting blocked grade crossings, publicizes those numbers, funds a National Academy of Sciences study of the worst-blocked crossings, and expands the Railroad Crossing Elimination grant program to $1.5 billion a year with priority for school bus routes.

It gives railroads 30 days, instead of longer windows, to submit post-accident toxology testing results and requires railroads to pay for the full cleanup costs of any accident involving their equipment.

analysis.who_pays: The largest freight railroads (Class I carriers) bear most of the cost: two-person crews on thousands of trains, new wayside defect detectors and maintenance, speed restrictions, safer tank cars, emergency response plans, staffing a blocked-crossing hotline, and fines up to $5 million per violation. Tank car owners and shippers face the cost of retrofitting or retiring older tank cars by the 2027 phase-out. Some of these costs are likely to be passed through to customers and shipping rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class I freight railroads and tank car owners

drawbacks.text: The two-person crew requirement grandfathers trains that already ran with fewer than two crew members before enactment, letting railroads keep those operations unless the Secretary finds they fall short of the safety level a two-person crew would provide — a substantial carve-out that railroads could invoke widely.

Many of the bill's central provisions are one- to two-year rulemakings rather than immediate rules, and several require compliance with Executive Order 12866 cost-benefit review, which gives regulated railroads multiple avenues to slow or soften the final standards.

The tank car phase-out can be delayed a full year to December 31, 2028 on the Secretary's finding of insufficient manufacturing capacity or significant impacts to interstate commerce, and the DOT-117 standard it phases in was itself the product of a phased timeline that critics considered too gradual.

Compliance costs for the largest railroads — crew pay, detector networks, tank car retrofits, and fines — will likely be passed through to freight customers and ultimately to consumer prices for goods moved by rail, and railroads argue mandates could shift freight to roads, which has a worse safety record per ton-mile.

The small railroads (Class II and III) get lower penalty caps and exemptions from some audit and hotline requirements, leaving a narrower but still-present gap in coverage on lines that carry hazardous materials too.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: the bill targets the specific failure modes behind recent deadly derailments — overheated bearings on long trains, thin-skinned tank cars carrying flammable liquids, and thin crews stretched over mile-plus trains — with enforcement teeth to match. The costs fall mostly on large, highly profitable railroads and on the tank car sector that built to older standards, though some will reach shippers and consumers. The main design weakness is that the crew-size grandfather clause and the slow rulemaking timelines give railroads room to delay compliance for years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (plus Science, Space, and Technology) and to its Railroads subcommittee on July 12, 2024, and no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Troy Nehls (R-TX) introduced the Railroad Safety Enhancement Act of 2024 on July 11, 2024, joined by an initial group of cosponsors from both parties including Representatives Seth Moulton, Emilia Sykes, Chris Deluzio, and Derrick Van Orden.

The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, and then to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee on July 12, 2024.

It gathered 33 cosponsors — 27 of 216 House Democrats and 6 of 224 House Republicans — but the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee never held a markup or vote, and the House never considered it before the 118th Congress ended.

The bill's provisions — two-person crews, wayside defect detector mandates, and tank car upgrades — closely track the safety response demanded after the February 2023 East Palestine, Ohio derailment; the parallel Railway Safety Act (S. 576) also failed to advance in the Senate during the 118th Congress, leaving none of the major rail safety legislation enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Class I freight railroads are better off: they avoided new two-person crew requirements, speed caps, defect detector mandates, tank car phase-outs, and fines of up to $5 million per violation that the bill would have imposed. Communities along rail lines continue to live without the crew, detector, and speed protections the bill would have provided.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.role: The major freight rail industry (BNSF, Union Pacific, CSX, Norfolk Southern and peers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory two-person crew requirements and other operating mandates during the 118th Congress rail safety debate, arguing crew size and similar rules should be set by labor agreements and cost-benefit analysis rather than statute.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 33 cosponsors split 27 Democrats and 6 Republicans alongside a Republican lead sponsor, so support was bipartisan — but with a Republican House majority, no committee vote was ever scheduled.

industries.note: The bill would impose two-person crews, 50/40 mph speed caps, defect detector networks with federal approval and fines, emergency response plans, a blocked-crossing hotline, and penalties up to $5 million per violation on the largest railroads. Railroads' interest in avoiding these operating and compliance costs runs against the safety protections the public would gain.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and retrofit shops
industries.note: The 2027 phase-out of older DOT-105/111/112/120 tank cars for flammable liquids unless they meet DOT-117 standards would force a wave of new car orders and retrofits. The bill also authorizes $5 million for tank car safety R&D and a GAO review of manufacturing capacity. Their gain comes directly from building the safer equipment the public needs.

industries.industry: Railcar telematics and sensor technology providers
industries.note: The bill authorizes $100 million a year for grants to railcar owners to install onboard telematics and gateway devices, plus a sensor development pilot program, prioritizing toxic-inhalation and flammable tank cars. Federal money flows to a private technology sector, but for monitoring equipment that improves hazard visibility for communities and responders.

industries.industry: Shortline and regional railroads (Class II and III)
industries.note: The bill gives small railroads lower penalty caps ($1,000-$200,000, up to $500,000 for severe violations), exempts them from most audits and allows waivers from the toll-free blocked-crossing hotline, easing compliance costs; but they remain subject to safety inspections and, if they carry hazmat, other requirements. Their burden is lighter than the Class I railroads' but not zero.
